papers.title: A high-speed and high-resolution 3D velocity map imaging system with a neuromorphic camera
papers.abstract: An improved camera-based 3D-velocity map imaging (VMI) system was demonstrated with a neuromorphic camera. We show a machine vision event-driven camera can achieve an unprecedented latency of 2 microseconds when detecting single ion/electron with a microchannel plate imaging detector, which boosts the speed of the momentum imaging system to more than 100 kHz, while the system with a conventional frame camera is limited to a few kHz. The high spatial resolution of the camera offers additional performance boost while maintaining excellent multi-hit capability and a high time resolution.

papers.title: Autonomous Multireference Quantum Chemistry with Artificial Intelligence Agents
papers.abstract: Accurately describing chemical reactions that involve strongly correlated electrons remains a major challenge in computational chemistry. Multireference electronic structure methods can address this challenge, but their application requires expert decisions that are di!cult to automate, particularly when the electronic structure changes as chemical bonds form and break. Here we introduce CASPER, an autonomously agentic workflow that performs multireference calculations along chemical reaction pathways. CASPER combines chemical knowledge, electronic structure calculations, and iterative assessment to identify chemically meaningful active spaces and maintain their consistency as bonds form and break. We demonstrate its capabilities on five transition-metal reactions, for which CASPER generates consistent multireference potential energy profiles with minimal human intervention. Importantly, in two reactions, CASPER identifies critical electronic-structure problems that an independent Claude session fails to recognize without the structured workflow. These include an electronic-state crossing and the exclusion of an orbital involved in bond breaking. Our results show the importance of combining language models with chemical knowledge and independent assessment of computational results. Beyond automating calculations, such agents have the potential to help researchers better understand the underlying physics and chemistry and open new opportunities for investigating complex chemical reactivity and generating high-quality quantum chemical data at scale.

papers.title: Auditing two-stage MS/MS molecular retrieval on MassSpecGym v1.5: Reranking gains, candidate priors and spectrum dependence
papers.abstract: Two-stage retrieval of molecular structures from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) can benefit from candidate reranking, but benchmark gains may also reflect candidate priors, replicate spectra, precursor mass, and training-set coverage. We audit a two-stage retrieval system on the official MassSpecGym v1.5 split (17,556 test spectra). A data-safe DreaMS encoder and composite molecular fingerprints provide an initial shortlist; a support-gated reranker combines pair scores, candidate-relative peak coverage, and mass-feasibility features. The final system achieves 31.05% Recall@1, a 10.05-point gain over its Stage 1 ensemble, while preserving its 72.62% Recall@20. Replacing the query spectrum with one from a different molecule matched on adduct and precursor mass reduces Recall@1 by 9.0 points (15.3 points under molecule-balanced weighting); nevertheless, a training-mean spectrum retains 13.75% Recall@1, indicating substantial spectrum-independent signal. Mass-feasibility features improve Recall@1 beyond score and coverage controls, while learned peak-fragment similarities do not outperform constant coverage. Errors cluster by molecule, and removing close training neighbours causes a large decline in Stage 1 shortlist recall among initially well-covered molecules. We conclude that candidate-relative mass-feasibility evidence improves front-rank retrieval and spectrum dependence, but does not establish learned structural discrimination or eliminate candidate priors. Evaluation should separately assess shortlist reachability, spectrum dependence, and molecule-level generalization.

papers.title: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
papers.abstract: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. Here we present a machine-learned classical density functional for ionic fluids that combines a symmetry-adapted neural free energy for short-range correlations with explicit long-range electrostatics. Trained on three-dimensional equilibrium densities and bulk correlations of the full-Coulomb restricted primitive model, a single functional transfers to charge-patterned particles and atomically structured electrodes. Around anisotropic charged solutes, it reproduces the ionic structure and mean forces from molecular dynamics, including reversals of the bare electrostatic force. At metal electrodes, self-consistent coupling to metal atoms captures the redistribution of ionic and electrode charge and the loading-dependent capacitance enhancement produced by steps and bumps. Combined with mobilities determined independently from bulk molecular dynamics, the same functional describes the main features of charging dynamics and resolves geometry-dependent spatial relaxation. This framework can be extended to more complex ionic fluids, enabling efficient exploration of how composition and geometry control structure and response.

papers.title: What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
papers.abstract: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

papers.title: Rare Event Analysis via Stochastic Optimal Control
papers.abstract: Rare events, from biomolecular conformational changes and phase transitions to chemical reactions, are central to many physical systems, yet extremely difficult to study computationally because unbiased simulations seldom produce them. Transition Path Theory provides a rigorous statistical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes the ensemble of reactive trajectories between two metastable states (reactant and product), and its central object, the committor function (the probability that the system next reaches the product rather than the reactant), encodes essential kinetic and thermodynamic information. We introduce a framework for committor estimation that builds on stochastic optimal control, with a principled formulation that grounds committor learning on capped hitting-time trajectories. In this framework the committor defines a feedback control, proportional to the gradient of its logarithm, that steers trajectories toward the reactive region, enabling sampling of reactive paths. As practical algorithms, we develop two training losses: a heuristic on-policy direct backpropagation loss and a principled off-policy Value Matching loss, for which we establish first-order optimality guarantees. Being off-policy, Value Matching can leverage simulated trajectories from alternative sampling processes and reuse them from a replay buffer, which enables efficient learning. In particular, we derive a reactive current-preserving sampling process that can accelerate exploration. On reversible and non-reversible dynamics, the framework yields more accurate committor estimates, reaction rates, and transition path samples than existing methods.

papers.title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
papers.abstract: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations for fluids have largely been developed in reduced-dimensional geometries. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional canonical equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential training labels. A functional learned from coarse three-dimensional density fields remains predictive at finer resolution, separating the sampling demands of training from the spatial resolution of subsequent predictions. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the potential of mean force between colloids due to solvent mediation, and adsorption isotherms in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that molecular dynamics equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.

papers.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.

papers.title: Trigonal Elliptic Coordinates on the Sphere and Some Applications
papers.abstract: We construct a theta-function parametrization of the unit sphere adapted to the eight trigonal directions. The construction follows from a cubic theta identity discussed by Bobek and admits an equivalent representation in Jacobi elliptic functions. The angular parameter and theta nome give a nonorthogonal coordinate system whose squared Cartesian components are related to the three-component Volterra chain. An algebraic change of angle, retaining the nome, yields orthogonal coordinates with explicit metric coefficients and a diagonal Laplace--Beltrami operator. We apply both parametrizations to the geometry of O'Brien's reduced Jahn--Teller model and give compact expressions for real spherical harmonics of degrees two and three. The orthogonal angle is the polar angle of an $E_g$ quadrupolar doublet, while one octupolar harmonic depends only on the nome within each octant.

papers.title: The replication-energy limit of PQG reduced-density-matrix theory from a single-fragment semidefinite program
papers.abstract: Variational two-electron reduced-density-matrix calculations are not size extensive: the energy per fragment can decrease when identical, strictly noninteracting fragments are replicated [M. Nakata and K. Yasuda, Phys. Rev. A 80, 042109 (2009)]. For the $P$, $Q$, and $G$ conditions (PQG) we prove the following. (i) The energy per fragment converges to the minimum of a semidefinite program (SDP) on one fragment. The limit is reached through negative interfragment covariances of order $1/(k-1)$ for $k$ replicas, which cancel the local electron number and spin fluctuations consistently with a global singlet. (ii) The energy per fragment is nonincreasing in the replica count. (iii) It reaches the limit exactly at a finite replica count. (iv) The defect is tied to the local electron-number variance: a sharp local electron number restores additivity without a spin constraint. (v) In chains of identical units the energy per unit has a limit that tends to the same minimum as the coupling vanishes. The key tool is that the $G$ condition [C. Garrod and J. K. Percus, J. Math. Phys. 5, 1756 (1964)] keeps the variances and covariances of one-body operators positive semidefinite without a representing state, so that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applies. PQG therefore admits explicitly constructed replicated points whose compensated local fluctuations lower the energy per fragment below the isolated value. Be, CH$_4$, N$_2$, and H$_2$O (STO-6G) and a four-site Hubbard fragment illustrate the results; in these examples the gap to the isolated value persists with three-index conditions $T_1$ and $T_2$.

papers.title: Strain-transfer at the Cu nanoparticle-Si(111) interface: static atomistic modelling and simulated Bragg CDI
papers.abstract: Substrate strain offers a route to control deformation in supported metallic nanoparticles, provided that interfacial coupling transmits the imposed loading into the particle. We assess this feasibility using five static Cu/Si(111) configurations spanning 0-2% biaxial tensile substrate strain. A 211,288-atom Cu particle is supported by a nominally 50 x 50 x 20 nm Si slab with its bottom 1 nm fixed, using the Jelinek modified embeddedatom potential. Relative to the relaxed supported 0% state, Cu-only local fits reveal heterogeneous, anisotropic deformation: particle-wide mean hydrostatic strain is negative at every nonzero loading, from -3.12 x 10-6 to -8.84 x 10-6, while the upper-particle mean varies nonmonotonically. Simulated Bragg CDI of Cu(111), obtained by inversion of known complex atomic scattering amplitudes, maps loading-dependent projected displacement and strain. The combined atomistic and Bragg CDI representations provide strong preliminary support for the feasibility of substrate-mediated strain transfer in this idealized system and identify spatial signatures for experimental investigation. Experiments remain indispensable to confirm transfer in real Cu/Si(111) nanoparticles and determine its magnitude.

papers.title: Ballistic propagation-mediated super-resolution light-element imaging: in-situ tracking dynamic hydrogen migration
papers.abstract: Transmission electrons - with few-picometer wavelengths - can theoretically resolve all atoms in solids. However, constrained by factors such as lens aberrations, Z-contrast dependence and poor temporal resolution, the scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) fails to tackle the long-standing challenge of hydrogen dynamics on atomic scale. Here, our experiment-guided simulations reveal that unlike heavy-atom imaging - governed by wave-based imaging process - ballistic propagation of particle-like electrons in Cs-corrected TEM enables super-resolution imaging (SRI) of light atoms, achieving a resolution down to 14 pm and a robust hydrogen contrast of ~24%. Our in-situ SRI study not only uncovers polymetric hydrogen aggregation in TiHx and H-LaAlO3, but also inter-site migration, rotational displacement of hydrogen species and collective hydrogen tunneling-induced polarization surge in the oxide. By exploiting the novel electron-matter interactions, our findings offer an unparalleled approach to probe hydrogen dynamics and establish accurate structure-property relationships in diverse functional materials.

papers.title: Coherent Control of Single-Photon Emission in Broadband Plasmonic Resonators
papers.abstract: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is challenging due to ultrafast relaxation induced by the broadband nature of the plasmonic near field. Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics theory, we demonstrate that an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field that is driven by a pulsed laser with frequency comb spectrum undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency comb components due to coherent accumulation, and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles with duration set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions are discussed for exponentially suppressing the probability of two or more emission events within the lifetime of the coupled emitter-nanocavity system. The spectral signatures of the optimal one-photon wavepackets are discussed. This work paves the way for the development of ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities.

papers.title: Systematically improvable semiclassical clustering for accurate and efficient quantum dynamics in large spin ensembles
papers.abstract: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies. While accurate methods for spin dynamics are limited to relatively small systems, the dissipative spin environments in real experiments typically involve orders of magnitude more spins. Semiclassical methods can reach these sizes, but their classical treatment of the bath cannot capture the sensor-bath entanglement that generates coherence revivals, especially under the application of refocusing pulses. Here, we resolve this tension. We introduce cluster spin-LSC, a method that clusters the sensor together with a few strongly coupled bath spins, treating them quantum mechanically in an otherwise classical spin bath. We show that our method is applicable to systems containing arbitrary spin species under dynamical decoupling pulse sequences. Our method converges systematically to the exact dynamics with cluster size, providing an internal consistency check when no exact benchmarks exist. We demonstrate that cluster spin-LSC recovers numerically exact coherence and population dynamics for a nitrogen-vacancy center and a molecular qubit, reducing day-long multi-GPU simulations to only minutes on a CPU. We further extend our method to systems with large spin baths that lie beyond the reach of exact methods. Our approach thus offers a scalable and systematically improvable route to accurately simulate the decoherence dynamics of sensors in realistic spin environments.

papers.title: Nonempirical Determination of the Optimal TAO-DFT Fictitious Temperature for Molecular Systems in the Lowest Singlet State
papers.abstract: Thermally-assisted-occupation density functional theory (TAO-DFT) [J.-D. Chai, J. Chem. Phys., 2012, ${\bf 136}$, 154104] has been developed to investigate the ground-state properties of large electronic systems exhibiting varying multi-reference (MR) character. As a central parameter in TAO-DFT, the fictitious temperature $\theta$ is closely linked to the degree of static correlation in an electronic system. While the conventional system-independent $\theta$-scheme is computationally efficient and broadly applicable, a fixed, preassigned $\theta$ can be overly large for single-reference (SR) systems yet too small for strongly MR systems. To overcome this limitation, we propose a nonempirical scheme based on spin-symmetry restoration to determine the optimal system-dependent fictitious temperature $\theta^{*}$ for molecular systems in their lowest singlet states. Across benchmark tests encompassing both MR systems (the bond dissociation of H$_{2}$, N$_{2}$, Li$_{2}$, and LiH, as well as the torsional rotation of twisted ethylene) and pure SR systems (the dissociation of He$_{2}$ and Ne$_{2}$), our nonempirical approach demonstrates superior overall accuracy compared with the conventional fixed-$\theta$ scheme. Furthermore, relative to standard Kohn-Sham density functional theory (TAO-DFT with $\theta = 0$), TAO-DFT employing $\theta^{*}$ yields substantial improvements for MR systems while preserving comparable accuracy in SR systems.

papers.title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation
papers.abstract: Conventional two-stage distillation first establishes a teacher through teacher-driven configuration exploration, a costly first stage for complex materials, and then uses its predictions to supervise students, potentially propagating teacher-label errors. Here, we propose distillation-driven teacher-student co-evolution (DICE), which uses a fast student to accelerate configuration exploration and replaces the fixed teacher-to-student sequence with alternating student and teacher updates. A representation-based support-assessment algorithm routes high-support configurations to teacher labelling and selects low-support configurations for density functional theory (DFT) calculations to update the teacher, thereby reducing the risk of teacher-label error propagation to students. Across Al2O3 (structural ceramics), yttria-stabilised zirconia (solid electrolytes) and MIL-120(Al) (a metal-organic framework), DICE develops reliable compact potentials using only 140-494 target DFT reference configurations per system; total recorded student exploration times per system are just 2.6-5.1% of the corresponding teacher-driven estimates. Combining computational efficiency with broad applicability across diverse material systems, DICE provides a practical route to developing reliable compact interatomic potentials.

papers.title: A response-based self-energy from equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory and its reduction to GW, GW+SOSEX, and GF2
papers.abstract: We construct a frequency-dependent one-particle correlation self-energy by coupling a reference Green's function to the neutral excitation response obtained from equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory with singles and doubles (EOM-CCSD). Direct, mixed direct-antisymmetrized, and fully antisymmetrized choices of the external interaction vertices define three approximations, all admitting an explicit spectral representation without numerical frequency integration. In the bare-state limit, the mixed and fully antisymmetrized forms recover second-order Green's-function theory (GF2), whereas the direct form retains only its ring contribution. With a direct random-phase approximation (RPA) response, the direct and mixed forms reduce to $G_0W_0$ and $G_0W_0$ plus second-order screened exchange (SOSEX), respectively. For molecular ionization potentials, replacing the RPA response by EOM-CCSD generally lowers the ionization energies, whereas introducing exchange at one external vertex raises them. These substantial opposing effects partially compensate, although the mixed approximation does not systematically improve upon conventional $G_0W_0$, either against IP-EOM-CCSD or QUESTDB reference energies (aug-cc-pVDZ mean absolute errors relative to the QUESTDB theoretical best estimates: 0.45 vs 0.36~eV). A third-order perturbative analysis reveals that the three approximations retain different contributions and weights of particle-hole diagrams while omitting explicit particle-particle and hole-hole ladder contributions and the static self-energy. In particular, the fully antisymmetrized form recovers GF2 at second order but assigns incorrect weights to its retained third-order diagrams. These findings highlight the importance of a balanced treatment of screening and vertex corrections in constructing accurate self-energy approximations.

papers.title: Efficient Spectra and Dynamics with Tangent-Space Chebyshev Tree Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: We present a tangent-space Chebyshev method (TaChe), which combines tree tensor network states with Chebyshev recursion and maximum entropy spectral analysis in a tree tensor network tangent space, for quantum many-body spectra and dynamics. Implemented tensor network state calculations in the tangent space of the ground state, the core advantage of TaChe is that it can substantially reduce the computational complexity, memory usage, and numerical instability associated with tensor network state compression. Implemented on the GPU platform, it produces accurate spectra with speedups of up to $46.8$ over the previous Chebyshev tensor network method and $13.7$ over one-site time-dependent variational principle propagation in the reported benchmarks. Applications to acetonitrile, thermal aggregate emission, finite-temperature charge transport on a \(6\times6\) lattice, and internal conversion in aggregates of up to 100 molecules demonstrate the efficiency and versatility of TaChe in simulating complex molecular systems.

papers.title: Intrinsic volume fraction can decouple from hydrodynamic size in p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels
papers.abstract: Quantifying the packing fraction of microgels is key to understanding their rheology and transport properties. Often, packing fractions are extrapolated from the hydrodynamic size and intrinsic volume fraction under the assumption that particle size and polymer volume change are proportional. Here, we test this assumption for p(N-isopropylacrylamide-co-acrylic acid) [p(NIPAm-co-AA)] microgels of two crosslinker concentrations (1 wt\% and 7 wt\% methylenebisacrylamide) using capillary viscometry and light scattering (static and dynamic) above and below the pKa of acrylic acid (AA). At pH 8, where AA is fully ionized, the microgels do not undergo a pronounced volume phase transition because electrostatic repulsion hinders thermal collapse, and both measures of hydrodynamic volume are equal. At pH 4, however, p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels are weakly charged and exhibit a volume phase transition near the lower critical solution temperature of pNIPAm; the magnitude of the size change is greater for the less-crosslinked microgel. Above the volume phase transition temperature, the volume change from hydrodynamic radius decouples from that from viscosity. The ratio of the radius of gyration and hydrodynamic radius R_g/R_h of p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels at high temperature exceeds the value theoretically predicted for homogeneous spheres and the deviation increases with the extent of crosslinking, suggesting that a non-uniform internal distribution of polymer gives rise to the anomalous decoupling at high temperatures. Our results indicate that care must be taken in extrapolating packing fractions for multi-responsive copolymer microgels, and suggest that copolymer composition and crosslink density may be used to tune bulk properties such as rheology through the internal microstructure.

papers.title: An informational interpretation of the reverse nonequilibrium molecular dynamics
papers.abstract: Reverse nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (RNEMD) is an efficient simulation method for determining transport coefficients. In this method, a flux is imposed by a seemingly artificial nonlocal exchange operation and the corresponding thermodynamic gradient is induced as a result, apparently reversing the usual force-flux causality. Although this method is well studied as a simulation technique, developing an information-thermodynamic interpretation of its Maxwell-demon-type operation and the associated apparent reversal of force-flux causality would provide a solid physical foundation for algorithms of this type. Here, we develop an information-reservoir interpretation for a representative RNEMD scheme for determining self-diffusivity. We show that the statistical bias of the information reservoir defines an information affinity that sustains a concentration gradient and a diffusive flux in the steady state. We further derive the linear transport coefficient corresponding to the information affinity in the linear response regime. Using the large deviation functional for the steady-state densities and currents, we also establish a fluctuation theorem for entropy production and the thermodynamic uncertainty relation linking entropy production to the fluctuations of the particle current. Computer simulations are performed to corroborate our theoretical results.

papers.title: Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo Simulations with Fast Ewald Summation for Calculating Individual Ionic Chemical Potentials
papers.abstract: We present a Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation method using fast Ewald summation to accurately and efficiently calculate the individual ionic excess chemical potentials of $\alpha_+:\alpha_-$ electrolyte solutions. By introducing a dynamic inner electrostatic potential that acts to penalize net charge fluctuations and maintain average charge neutrality ($\langle Q_t \rangle = 0$), the method enables single-ion GCMC trial moves without sacrificing convergence speed or breaking thermodynamic consistency. Unlike the Widom particle insertion method---which suffers from severe phase-space sampling bottlenecks and requires separate virtual insertions for each ionic species---the Donnan GCMC protocol simultaneously yields the individual excess chemical potentials $\mu_+^{\text{ex}}$ and $\mu_-^{\text{ex}}$ corresponding to a resulting bulk concentration $c_b$ with rapid numerical convergence. Varying the reference activity parameter $c_r$ allows us to efficiently construct the complete $\mu_\pm^{\text{ex}}(c_b)$ curves. Comparison with the Mean Spherical Approximation (MSA) demonstrates excellent agreement for size-symmetric electrolytes, while highlighting the failure of linear-response theories for size-asymmetric ions where electrostatic correlations and cavity effects become strongly coupled.

papers.title: Electric polarizabilities with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: While projector quantum Monte Carlo methods are known for producing accurate ground-state energies, the prediction of other properties that encode the electronic response to applied electric and magnetic fields has historically been challenging. In this work we demonstrate that the electric (static) polarizability tensor, which is formally a second-derivative of the energy with respect to electric fields, can be efficiently computed with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo using a correlated sampling finite-difference strategy. With simple Hartree-Fock trial wave functions, we investigate a series of small molecules (some of which are difficult for approximate density functionals), polyacenes of increasing size, and ferrocene as a representative organometallic complex. The methodology is scalable to relatively large molecules involving thousands of basis functions, and with appropriate trial wave functions remains robust for strongly correlated electronic states, as we show for the stretched dinitrogen molecule. This work opens the door to the computation of a host of other second-order molecular properties with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, which will inform the ongoing search for optimal trial wave functions and extend benchmark-quality training data sets for the refinement of semi-empirical and machine learning models for quantum chemistry and molecular simulation.

papers.title: Using potential derivatives to reduce the cost of rectangular collocation: a general and versatile approach for computational vibrational spectroscopy without a potential energy surface
papers.abstract: We modify the exact Cartesian kinetic energy operator, rectangular collocation approach of Manzhos and Carrington [J. Chem. Phys. 145 (2016) 224110] by using information contained in potential derivatives to decrease the number of required potential points. We show that this makes it possible to substantially reduce the number of collocation points, which is important, in particular, when energies are computed directly ab initio. Vibrational band intensities are also computed. We first demonstrate the method on Cl2CO and compare to high-accuracy Smolyak collocation calculations on an accurate potential energy surface (PES). Sub-cm-1 accuracy is obtained with a few thousand Gaussian basis functions and potential points. A spectrum computed directly from DFT energies and a comparison to GVPT2 (generalized vibrational perturbation theory) are also presented. We then consider LiCO2 as a more anharmonic case, for which a quartic force field potential is less reliable, and which also serves as a surrogate model for a catalytic system (mimicking CO2 bond weakening by charge donation). The rectangular collocation method is used to compute the spectrum of LiCO2 directly from ab initio energies and to compare to GVPT2. The method is implemented as a Claude Skill and is easily usable by anyone on any molecule. The method is a general and versatile tool for anharmonic computational vibrational spectroscopy. It does not require a PES and no coupling is neglected.

papers.title: State of Understanding of High-speed Combustion: Can the Detonation Structure in Fuel-Air Mixtures Be Predicted?
papers.abstract: (Abridged) High-speed reacting flows are central to many natural and practical systems, from detonation-based propulsion to various astrophysical phenomena. Here we discuss the limitations in our understanding of high-speed combustion by asking how well modern state-of-the-art physicochemical and computational models can predict the properties of a freely propagating detonation. We present a systematic survey of eleven fuel/air mixtures, from hydrogen, methane, acetylene, and ethylene to JP-10 and n-dodecane jet fuels, at a range of upstream pressures, temperatures, and equivalence ratios. Detonation properties are analyzed using prior numerical studies in the literature, as well as the multi-dimensional, high-fidelity simulations performed in this work, which employ modern multi-step kinetics based on the FFCM/HyChem families of reaction mechanisms. We show that simulations reproduce experimental cell sizes in H$_2$/air at sub-atmospheric pressures or elevated upstream temperatures, yet at the atmospheric conditions, disagreement in the predicted cell sizes is a factor of 3 - 6 at stoichiometric composition and much more severe in lean mixtures. Hydrocarbon fuels show comparable or even larger discrepancies. We argue that such disagreement cannot be ascribed solely to the computational factors, in particular, numerical resolution even at the continuum limit. We analyze the thermodynamic state space occupied by detonations in various mixtures, describe the predicted chemical properties in various regions of the state space, in particular ignition delays and their temperature sensitivity, and consider how well modern chemical kinetics mechanisms are constrained at these conditions by the direct ignition delay measurements. We further assess the proposed role of vibrational non-equilibrium and demonstrate that the current evidence is inconclusive. Finally, we summarize key open questions.

papers.title: Adaptive Multiset Tree Tensor Networks for Large-Scale Exciton Dynamics
papers.abstract: Electronic excitations coupled to vibrational environments play an important role in charge and energy transport in molecular materials. Multiset tree tensor networks provide an efficient ansatz for the dynamics of such systems by allowing different electronic configurations to develop independent environmental correlations. However, typical implementations use fixed bond dimensions, significantly limiting the accessible system size and hence their predictive capabilities for large scale systems. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the adaptive multiset tree tensor network (AMTTN) approach, in which the bond dimensions of each configuration are adapted independently using a local energy variance based expansion scheme. Additionally, configurations can be temporarily frozen whenever they are predicted to remain weakly populated throughout a timestep. For the one-dimensional Holstein model, AMTTN reproduces converged exciton dynamics one to two orders of magnitude faster than fixed bond dimension multiset methods, with the dominant cost determined by the dynamically active region with only weak residual dependence on the lattice size. For a P3HT:PCBM heterojunction, it enables simulations of a model containing 52 oligothiophene units avoiding finite size effects occurring on dynamically relevant time scales, which lead to the previously studied 13 unit model substantially overestimating long time populations of bound charge separated states. Our results show that AMTTN provides a practical method for obtaining converged quantum dynamics simulations of challenging excitonic and non-adiabatic systems for which conventional multiset approaches are prohibitively expensive.

papers.title: Where does a molecule begin? Threshold masses of three-particle Coulomb systems and a predictive theory of their Born-Oppenheimer offsets
papers.abstract: The Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation serves as the foundational framework for the contemporary concept of molecular structure, which is central to chemistry and the molecular sciences. Its principal assumption is the treatment of nuclei as infinitely heavy particles. In this work, we test the boundaries of the BO approximation by examining systems with variable nuclear masses to investigate the emergence of molecular structure. We examine the three-particle family {X^+,X^+,e^-} as a function of the mass ratio M = m_X/m_e, using deterministic variational calculations and the exact BO approximation. We accurately compute the threshold masses of all 23 excited levels bound below M = 100 with certified upper bounds. The BO approximation places every one of them too late by a nearly constant amount, 1.2 to 1.6 (0.23 to 0.54 with the adiabatic correction). We explain this constancy with a parameter-free theory, and test it with predictions frozen before the exact calculations: 18 of 18 symmetric levels pass (typical miss 0.003). For unequal nuclear masses none of 7 levels falls within the band, but the theory still captures over 90% of the offset. Where does a molecule begin? The ground state changes character gradually, over a crossover 2.3 decades wide in M. The sharp landmarks are the threshold masses: the first rotational level binds at M = 4.208, in the ortho-type nuclear-spin species, and the first vibrational level at M = 9.526; BO places them at 5.54 and 11.08. Thus, the BO picture orders the spectrum correctly at finite mass and shifts it by an amount that can be computed.

papers.title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders
papers.abstract: Nonpremixed flames in the forward stagnation region of porous cylinders are classically described by the first-order stagnation-point boundary layer, which neglects the effects of surface curvature and boundary-layer displacement. In the present work, the description is extended to second order for a porous parabolic cylinder using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. The flame is assumed to be a sheet detached from the porous wall with unity Lewis numbers, and the model accounts for thermal expansion and displacement of the entire reacting layer. The expansion is verified against laminar Navier-Stokes solutions of the same idealized problem, and in the resolved cases the two-term errors decrease approximately as the square of the expansion parameter. At Reynolds numbers typical of laboratory-scale burners, curvature and displacement move the flame away from the wall and reduce the scalar dissipation rate, wall shear, and wall heat flux, whereas the flame temperature changes little. These effects increase with injection, and displacement contributes more over a longer porous section. The second-order terms considerably reduce the errors of the first-order theory in the flame stand-off distance and the scalar dissipation rate.

papers.title: Handed Ultrafast Dynamics in Chiral Cyanine Nanotubes
papers.abstract: We detect helicity-dependent excited state relaxation in a chiral exciton system. Using L-histidine as a chiral inducer, we prepared unbundled, double-walled J-aggregrate nanotubes of an amphiphilic cyanine dye with a net handedness, which gives a large circular dichroism dissymmetry factor ($g_{abs} = 3.6 \times 10^{-2}$). With two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy and circularly polarized pump pulses, we find that the relaxation rates of longitudinal excitons depend on pump helicity (4.5 $ps^{-1}$ for $\langle \textit{RRXX} \rangle$ vs 6 $ps^{-1}$ for $\langle \textit{LLXX} \rangle$, a difference of about 30%) and is the same in the inner and outer tubes. Transverse excitons show no significant dependence. Chirality and pump helicity therefore bias exciton relaxation on the femtosecond timescale for excitons delocalized along the helical structure.

papers.title: RxnScope: Accurate joint generation of product and transition-state pairs from reactants via flow matching
papers.abstract: Reaction networks are central to understanding chemical reactivity and guiding reaction design. Constructing them when products are unknown remains a major challenge in computational chemistry, requiring the identification of products and their corresponding transition states (TSs) across elementary steps. Here, we introduce RxnScope, a flow-matching framework that jointly generates paired product-TS geometries from reactants, conditioned on a potentially reactive region. Directed product-to-TS coupling allows evolving rather than fixed product geometries to guide TS generation, while paired outputs enable product-topology ranking to prioritize candidates for validation. RxnScope recovered and validated 95.8% of reference pathways on Transition1x, performed robustly on multicomponent reactions and enabled multistep pathway exploration. In automatic reaction discovery, it achieved low-energy pathway coverage comparable to that of the single-ended growing string method while using only about 2% of its computational cost. These results establish joint product-TS generation as a new strategy for exploring reaction networks from reactants.

papers.title: Restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham theory for arbitrary genealogical spin coupling
papers.abstract: We introduce a generalization of restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) theory to a single configuration state function (CSF) with arbitrary genealogical spin coupling. This CSF-ROKS theory establishes a spin-pure density functional extension of the recently developed CSF-based restricted open-shell Hartree-Fock (CSF-ROHF) theory, providing a computationally efficient route to incorporate dynamic electron correlation. The energy is expressed as a weighted sum over unrestricted determinants built from a common set of restricted orbitals, and the number of determinants grows quadratically with the number of open shells. Numerical calculations for N$_2$ and the polyacene series show that CSF-ROKS solutions retain chemically interpretable character. Exchange-correlation functionals preferentially stabilize low-seniority configurations, shifting the onset of polyradical character in polyacenes to longer chains than predicted by CSF-ROHF. Furthermore, CSF-ROKS can be used to target state-specific spin-pure excitations in the vinyl and allyl radicals, and the [Cr(ddpd)$_2$]$^{3+}$ molecular ruby. However, CSF-ROKS incorrectly predicts ferromagnetic coupling in a set of bridged transition metal dimers, indicating that kinetic exchange requires more advanced correlated methods.
